issues.legal_issue: A deceased person's statement against proprietary interest is admissible only when the person knew it was against that interest.
material_facts: A deceased woman had stated in an earlier mortgage suit that her husband died before his father.
The statement placed her in the position of the widow of a predeceased son, who had no proprietary interest in her father-in-law's property under the law then applicable.
There was no family dispute when she made the statement, and the Court found it was made consciously and not at another family member's instigation.
issues.conclusion: The statement was admissible under section 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, as evidence against the deceased woman's proprietary interest; her knowledge that it was adverse could be inferred from the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a deceased person's statement against that person's pecuniary or proprietary interest is admissible, but the rationale for admitting it applies only if the person knew it was against that interest. Whether the person had that knowledge is a question of fact, generally determined from the circumstances. The Court relied on Srimati Savitri Debi v. Raman Bijoy, Tucker v. Oldburry Urban District Council, and Ward v. H. S. Pitt.

rule.if: civil_property_proceeding and declarant_is_dead and statement_is_against_declarants_proprietary_interest and declarant_knew_statement_was_adverse

predicates.civil_property_proceeding: The statement is offered in a proceeding concerning rights in property.
predicates.declarant_is_dead: The person who made the statement has died.
predicates.statement_is_against_declarants_propriet: The statement, if true, places its maker at a disadvantage in claiming or holding property.
predicates.declarant_knew_statement_was_adverse: The maker knew the statement was against their proprietary interest, as shown by the circumstances in which it was made.

issues.definition: When a deceased person knowingly made a statement adverse to their proprietary interest in a property proceeding, that statement is admissible evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A later statement in a gift document that only implies a different chronology does not outweigh an earlier statement made before a family dispute when the earlier statement directly addresses the chronology.
material_facts: In an earlier suit brought before any family trouble, a woman directly stated that her husband died before his father.

A later gift document did not expressly state that her husband died after his father; it stated that she and her co-widow took possession after his death, from which that chronology was said to be implied.
The gift document was made when the family situation had become troubled and asserted the maker's title to the property.
issues.conclusion: Assuming the later statements were admissible under section 158 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, they did not directly contradict the earlier statement and had little value; the earlier statement carried greater weight because it was made when there was no family dispute.
issues.legal_principle: Section 158 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, permits matters that could have been proved in cross-examination to be proved to contradict or corroborate a statement relevant under section 32 or 33. The Court assumed the gift-document statements could be admitted for that purpose, but held that the document contained no categorical statement contradicting the earlier account and that the circumstances and timing gave the earlier statement greater weight.

rule.if: civil_property_proceeding and earlier_statement_directly_addresses_chronology and earlier_statement_made_before_family_dispute and later_gift_document_only_implies_conflicting_chronology and later_document_supports_own_title

predicates.civil_property_proceeding: The competing statements are considered in a proceeding concerning rights in property.
predicates.earlier_statement_directly_addresses_chr: The earlier statement expressly describes the order in which relevant deaths occurred.
predicates.earlier_statement_made_before_family_dis: The earlier statement was made when there was no family dispute about the property.
predicates.later_gift_document_only_implies_conflic: The later gift document does not expressly state the disputed chronology but supports an inference about it.
predicates.later_document_supports_own_title: The maker included the later account in a document asserting a basis for transferring property.

issues.definition: Where an undisputed earlier statement directly addresses chronology and a later title-supporting document only implies a conflicting chronology, the earlier statement carries greater weight.

issues.legal_issue: A person who disappeared and was not heard from for more than seven years was presumed dead, allowing the property of which he was the last male holder to pass to the persons entitled through him.
material_facts: A man left his village and disappeared after his son died.
He had not been heard of for more than seven years after disappearing.
The Court found that the respondents were entitled to the property of which he was the last male holder.
issues.conclusion: The Court presumed the missing man dead and held that the respondents were entitled to the property of which he was the last male holder.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the presumption of death where a person had not been heard of for more than seven years after disappearing, and treated the respondents as entitled to the property of which that person was the last male holder.

rule.if: property_succession_proceeding and person_disappeared and person_not_heard_of_for_more_than_seven_years and person_was_last_male_holder_of_property

predicates.property_succession_proceeding: The proceeding concerns who is entitled to property through succession.
predicates.person_disappeared: The person left their usual community and could not be found thereafter.
predicates.person_not_heard_of_for_more_than_seven_: No one heard from the person for more than seven years after the disappearance.
predicates.person_was_last_male_holder_of_property: The person was the last male holder of the property in dispute.

issues.definition: In a property succession proceeding, if the last male holder disappeared and was not heard from for more than seven years, the person is presumed dead and successors are entitled to the property.
